Image Processing

An analog image is modelled by f:R2→Rf: R^2 \rarr Rf:R2→R﻿, meanwhile a digital one by f:Z2→Zf: Z^2 \rarr Zf:Z2→Z﻿

  • The codomain f(x,y)f(x, y)f(x,y)﻿ is called intensity
  • xxx﻿ and yyy﻿ are called spatial parameters, and in case of digital images pixels or picture elements f[x,y]f[x, y]f[x,y]﻿ vs f(x,y)f(x, y)f(x,y)﻿

Typically the intensity is encoded by a certain number of bits, called bit depth (unsigned int)

  • A gray scale image is defined by f:Z2→{0,...,2n−1}f: Z^2 \rarr \{0, ..., 2^n-1\}f:Z2→{0,...,2n−1}﻿
  • If n=1n=1n=1﻿ we will have a binary image (black and white)

A multi-sectral image is an image with d>1d>1d>1﻿, defined by: f:Z2→Zdf:Z^2 \rarr Z^df:Z2→Zd﻿

  • A couloured image has d=3d=3d=3﻿
  • dd d﻿ is also called the number of channels
  • if d=3d=3 d=3﻿ and n=8n=8n=8﻿ we get 2242^{24}224﻿ colours (16.7 millions)

Filters

A filter (or system) is a black box that converts an input image f[x,y]f[x,y]f[x,y]﻿ into an output image g[x,y]g[x,y]g[x,y]﻿

  • A filter is uniquely identified by its filter operator SSS﻿
  • A filter operator SSS﻿, referred to as filter, is a mapping from the set of possible input images to the outputs g[x,y]=S(f[x,y])g[x,y] = S(f[x,y])g[x,y]=S(f[x,y])﻿

Filters property

  1. Additivity: S(f[x,y]+g[x,y])=S(f[x,y])+S(g[x,y])S(f[x, y]+g[x, y]) = S(f[x, y]) + S(g[x, y])S(f[x,y]+g[x,y])=S(f[x,y])+S(g[x,y])﻿
  1. Homogeneity: S(αf[x,y])=αS(f[x,y])S(\alpha f[x, y]) = \alpha S(f[x, y])S(αf[x,y])=αS(f[x,y])﻿
  1. Superposition: S(αf[x,y]+βg[x,y])=αS(f[x,y])+βS(g[x,y])S(\alpha f[x, y] + \beta g[x, y]) = \alpha S(f[x, y]) + \beta S(g[x, y])S(αf[x,y]+βg[x,y])=αS(f[x,y])+βS(g[x,y])﻿ with α,β∈R\alpha, \beta \in Rα,β∈R﻿
    • By appling 1 and 2
    • Linear filter
  1. Shift invariance: g[x−x0,y−y0]=S(f[x−x0,y−y0])g[x-x_0, y-y_0] = S(f[x-x_0, y-y_0])g[x−x0​,y−y0​]=S(f[x−x0​,y−y0​])﻿
    • If it is also linear is called LSI filters (our eyes are a linear shift invariant filter)

There are two main types of filters:

  1. Smoothing filters → where the ∑hij=1\sum h_{ij}= 1∑hij​=1﻿ (preserve average intensity)
    1. Moving average filters
  1. Differentiating kernels → where the ∑hij=0\sum h_{ij} = 0∑hij​=0﻿ (gives zero in constant regions)

An image of shape Ih×IvI_h × I_vIh​×Iv​﻿ convolved with a kernel of shape Kh×KvK_h ×K_vKh​×Kv​﻿ will produce an output image of shape (Ih−Kh+1)×(Iv−Kv+1)(I_h − K_h +1)×(I_v −K_v +1)(Ih​−Kh​+1)×(Iv​−Kv​+1)﻿

To avoid that, the input image is typically “artificially enlarged” with padding, in such a way that the output image will maintain a shape Ih×IvI_h × I_vIh​×Iv​﻿, preserving edge information.

By applying a padding of php_hph​﻿ pixels horizontally and pvp_vpv​﻿ pixels vertically, the input image will have size (Ih+ph)×(Iv+pv)(I_h + p_h) × (I_v + p_v)(Ih​+ph​)×(Iv​+pv​)﻿ and the output image will have size (Ih−Kh+ph+1)×(Iv−Kv+pv+1)(I_h − K_h + p_h +1) × (I_v − K_v + p_v +1)(Ih​−Kh​+ph​+1)×(Iv​−Kv​+pv​+1)﻿.

A common choice for padding is ph=Kh−1p_h = K_h −1ph​=Kh​−1﻿ and pv=Kv−1p_v = K_v −1pv​=Kv​−1﻿

The filling can be done in different ways:

  1. Constant
  1. Extended → value of the closest border
  1. Mirror

Computational complexity for a single pixel [x,y][x, y][x,y]﻿ is O(m×n)O(m\times n)O(m×n)﻿

  • Too high considering the number of pixels in my image

Separeble Kernel: A 2D discrete kernel h[x,y]∈Rm×nh[x, y] \in R^{m\times n}h[x,y]∈Rm×n﻿ is separable if there are two 1D kernels h1[x]∈Rmh_1[x] \in R^mh1​[x]∈Rm﻿ and h2[y]∈Rnh_2[y] \in R^nh2​[y]∈Rn﻿ such that h[x,y]=h1[x]∗h2[y]h[x, y] =h_1[x]*h_2[y]h[x,y]=h1​[x]∗h2​[y]﻿

  • hhh﻿ is separable iif rank(h)=1\text{rank}(h)=1rank(h)=1﻿
    • every row is a scalar multiple of every other
    • every column is a scalr multiple of every other
  • Writing the vertical kernel first leads to the equivalence with outer product

  • O(m+n)O(m+n)O(m+n)﻿

Gaussian Filters

Discrete Gaussian functions are defined on a discrete but unlimited domain, namely Z2Z^2Z2﻿.

  • In order to use them in image processing, we need to synthesise a finite version → define them on a limited domain.

A gaussian filter is a finite and smoothing LSI filter whose impulse response approximated a discreate gaussian function
